summary.summary: Powys's Q4 report to 31 March 2026 shows total borrowing down £5.61m over the year to £362.03m even after £25m of new PWLB in Q4, with the CFR closing at £453.34m — £22.7m below the original estimate because capital schemes were reprofiled and extra Welsh Government grants landed. Financing costs came in at 3.8% of net revenue against 4.0% planned, but the report is explicit that the deferred borrowing 'will still be required in the future': the CFR is forecast to reach £614.20m by March 2028. The council was an active short-term lender to other authorities (£35.32m across six loans in Q4, all repaid by March 2026). Aged sundry debt rose £3.0m in the quarter to £15.51m, 73% of the over-three-month debt being hard-to-collect social care charges; all treasury prudential indicators were complied with.

signals.headline: Total borrowing fell £5.61m in 2025/26 to £362.03m at 31 March 2026 despite £25m of new PWLB in Q4; financing costs 3.8% of net revenue (£13.94m) vs 4.0% in the approved strategy
signals.why: A year of modest deleveraging with capital financing costs inside plan, helped by reprofiling and additional Welsh Government grants.

signals.headline: CFR forecast to rise from £453.34m at 31 March 2026 to £516.13m by March 2027 and £614.20m by March 2028 (+£161m in two years); the report states deferred borrowing 'will still be required in the future'
signals.why: This year's saving is a deferral, not an avoidance — the capital programme implies substantial new external borrowing at forecast PWLB rates above 5%.

findings.headline: General Fund reserve stands at exactly the 4% policy minimum (£12.3 million) with no buffer, while the council remains under-borrowed and borrowing costs have risen
findings.detail: Powys's General Fund reserve is £12.3 million, which equals 4.3% of the net revenue budget — the council's stated minimum threshold. While the council notes the reserve has increased by £0.8 million, this increase reflects only a larger revenue base, leaving no safety buffer above policy minimum. Simultaneously, the council 'remains under-borrowed as we continue to utilise our cash reserves to underpin our cashflow' but notes 'the cost of borrowing has risen.' This creates a timing trap: as reserves approach or fall below minimum (schools are already drawing £186k), the council will need to move to borrowing at higher cost.
findings.matters: A council with reserves at minimum policy level has no flexibility for unexpected pressures or funding reductions. Any further deterioration will breach reserves policy and trigger external intervention. Combined with the £28.8m medium-term gap, this signals the council is approaching the edge of its financial envelope. For lenders, reserves at minimum + rising borrowing costs + medium-term deficit = refinancing risk.
findings.figures: General Fund reserve £12.3m (4.3% of net revenue budget); minimum policy level 4%; reserve increase from prior year £0.8m
findings.quote: The Council remains under-borrowed as we continue to utilise our cash reserves to underpin our cashflow. We can borrow both in the short to medium or longer term, but the cost of borrowing has risen.

findings.headline: The council faces a £9.7 million funding gap in 2027-28 and a cumulative £28.8 million gap through 2030-31, with the Section 151 Officer warning that financial pressure will 'outweigh the funding available'
findings.detail: Powys's Medium-Term Financial Strategy identifies a funding gap of £9.7 million for 2027-28 and a cumulative gap of £28.8 million through 2030-31 'as a best-case scenario.' The Section 151 Officer has stated: 'Our Medium Term Financial Strategy continues to be extremely challenging with a significant budget gap of at least £28.8 million over the next 4 years as the financial pressure we continue to face is likely to outweigh the funding available.' No solution to this gap is yet identified; the officer notes that 'work on the development of proposals for 2027-28 to 2031-32 is already underway', signalling no quick fix exists.
findings.matters: A cumulative £28.8 million gap over four years, with no identified solution, is a sustainability crisis. This is not a single-year pressure or a technical forecast adjustment — it is a statement that the council's spending trajectory is unsustainable relative to funding. For lenders, this signals potential default risk in the medium term unless dramatic service cuts or spending cuts occur.
findings.quote: The MTFS published alongside the budget in February shows a funding gap of £9.7 million in 2027-28 and a cumulative funding gap by 2030-31 estimated at £28.8 million as a best-case scenario.

findings.headline: 23 schools are in financial deficit including one secondary with a £6.5 million projected deficit, and schools collectively are drawing £186k from reserves instead of building them
findings.detail: At Q1, 23 schools are projected to end the year in deficit (7 secondary schools, 13 primary, 2 all-age, 1 special), with a combined projected deficit of £7.181 million. One secondary school alone projects a deficit of £6.510 million. Rather than contributing to reserves, schools are expected to draw £186k from reserves by year-end (against a budgeted £2k contribution). While the council notes this is 'significantly improved' from the original budget submissions (which projected £358k draw), it still signals schools are collectively spending faster than they are funded. The council has created specific virements to clear accumulated deficits at Crickhowell High School (£374k for sports facilities, £68k for library).
findings.matters: Multiple schools in persistent deficit is a governance failure. A single secondary school deficit of £6.5m is a crisis-level problem for a council that must intervene. For lenders, schools deficits signal either underfunding in the formula, poor cost control, or both — and they consume council reserves and management time.
findings.figures: 23 schools in deficit; secondary school deficit of £6.510m; total school deficit of £7.181m; projected year-end reserve draw £186k; virements to clear Crickhowell deficits: £374k + £68k
findings.quote: Schools are collectively budgeting a £2k contribution to reserves, but at Quarter 1 a further projected draw of reserves of £186k is now expected by year end on 31 March 2027.

findings.headline: Children's Services is £418k overspent and facing a national shortage of placements driving up costs faster than the council can manage demand
findings.detail: Children's Services is forecasting a £418k overspend at Q1 due to 'continued pressure from high-cost out-of-county placements, increasing complexity of need, and increased demand at the front door.' The service explicitly notes 'a national shortage of placements', which is forcing Powys to compete for capacity and accept higher per-placement costs. The service holds £1.419 million of assured savings but acknowledges these remain 'subject to active monitoring' and faces 'demand-led pressures' that are outside its control.
findings.matters: Like Adult Services, this reflects a market problem (national shortage) combined with rising need. The council has limited control over placement availability or cost. For lenders, this is a second high-need, under-funded service showing structural deterioration.
findings.figures: Q1 projected overspend £418k; £1.419m assured cost reductions still at risk
findings.quote: Children's Services is forecasting a £418k projected overspend at end of Quarter 1 based on actuals and forecasted expenditure. This position is mainly driven by continued pressure from high-cost out-of-county placements, increasing complexity of need, and increased demand at the front door, which is placing additional pressure on assessment, intervention and placement budgets.

findings.headline: Adult Services is £5.4 million gross overspend driven by 32% surge in domiciliary care demand and nursing home cost inflation that the council cannot control
findings.detail: Adult Services reported a £5.424 million gross overspend at Q1. Even after assured savings of £4.539 million, the service will run £885k over budget. The driver is structural: domiciliary care hours surged 32% in five months (from 9,056 in April 2025 to 12,001 in June 2026), with people supported jumping from 599 to 746. The service notes that nursing home providers are stating the Funded Nursing Care rate 'is insufficient and does not cover their costs.' This is forcing out-of-county spot purchases 'at increased rates often above the host authority rates', particularly in mid and north Powys where local nursing provision cannot meet demand. The service is managing this year through prevention and repatriation but identifies this as ongoing structural pressure.
findings.matters: This is not a one-year budget blip but an aging-population problem the council cannot close with efficiency alone. Higher care complexity, workforce shortages forcing agency costs, and insufficient FNC rates mean placement costs will keep rising faster than funding. For lenders, this is a high-risk, under-funded service that deteriorates as demographics shift.
findings.figures: Gross overspend £5.424m; domiciliary care hours 9,056 (Apr-25) to 12,001 (Jun-26), +32%; people supported 599 to 746, +24%; net overspend after assured savings £885k (0.8% of £111.7m budget)
findings.quote: The forecast outturn at the end of Quarter 1 (period 3), 30th June 2026, is a £5.424 million overspend. Our ageing population with increased complexity of need is outstripping nursing provision within the county and forcing us to spot purchase out of county placements at increased rates often above the host authority rates.
